author: Tom Huntington Arts Correspondent
title: 'A reliable and transcendent heartbeat festival': Grace Potter brings back Grand Point North | Rutland Reader | rutlandherald.com
text:
After a return of sorts last year as a four-day concert series, the Grand Point North music festival — an annual two-day soiree that had become one of Vermont’s marquee music events during its storied nine-year run in the 2010s — will finally celebrate its 10th anniversary Sept. 12 and 13 at Burlington’s Waterfront Park.
Presented by Fayston native Grace Potter and Burlington-based concert promoter Higher Ground, the Grand Point North music festival will once again be headlined by Potter and her band, who on Friday will perform with the Vermont Symphony Orchestra.
Grand Point North includes a third show, which is part of the concert series and features rock/jam band heavyweights Goose playing a sold-out show on Sept. 14.
“Now it’s back to being the festival,” said Potter in a recent video call from her home in Fayston, a 120-acre farm that she and her husband, the renowned producer Eric Valentine, bought in 2020. Last year’s concert series “was sort of the caveat that we had to jump through to get back to the waterfront, which is the iconic location.”
“That’s what took so many years for us to get it back on board,” she explained, citing high costs, staffing needs and technical issues related to insurance as deterrents to the lakeside location. “The waterfront is a very expensive place to throw a music festival.”
“The entrée back into it being a concert series was a safer bet for that first reentry,” said Potter, adding: “Higher Ground will continue to do their concert series, but Grand Point North will be its own standalone festival now.”
While Higher Ground is still a partner in the Grand Point North music festival, this year’s fest will be run by Potter’s Grand Point Foundation, a nonprofit organization she created last year to support the arts and culture in Vermont.
“Nothing’s changed except that, on her end, she’s removed any economic motivation around the two days she performs,” stated Alex Crothers, co-owner of Higher Ground, via email in June. “I still need to balance an overall budget, but Grace’s piece of this can exist in a more cerebral place.”
For her part, Potter is happy to be the “vision quest person” in the festival equation.
“That is why the foundation needed to be a part of it, because … it’s truly a public service and it always has been in my mind,” she said. “I want to have a reliable and transcendent heartbeat festival that is just bringing up all the things about Vermont that I love and care about.”
‘It’s not just about me’
Friday night’s lineup includes fast-rising Nashville-based country artist Brittney Spencer along with such Burlington area bands as surf-rock trio The Wet Ones! femme punk group Burly Girlies and singer-songwriter Grace Palmer.
Saturday features New York City indie soul-pop trio Melt, Brooklyn psych-rock collective ISTA, Brattleboro punk band Slob Drop, Burlington/Miami rapper Heady Betty and Brattleboro synth-pop artist Dutch Experts, the solo project of Hannah Hoffman.
While Vermont bands have been part of Grand Point North since its inception, this year’s plethora of Green Mountain State artists in the lineup is palpable.
“It was a very specific focal point for me,” said Potter. “Not just because of the foundation, but also because I really feel called to bring Burlington back to center and focus in on these pillar, badass bands.”
“It’s just, like, why didn’t we do this years ago?” she added. “There are so many great bands.”
Potter’s Friday night performance with the VSO comes on the heels of two sold-out shows together in March at the Paramount Theatre in Rutland and The Flynn in Burlington, which she described as “one of the most transcendent experiences.”
“It was like being in a movie, like a slow-motion silent film with the best orchestra playing behind you,” she said. “I just really loved how boundless the set allowed me to be as a performer. It freed me up to embrace that more cinematic mind that I always have.”
“When I close my eyes, I see a movie in every song that I sing,” she added. “But when I’m with the orchestra, I don’t have to close my eyes. It’s all around me.”
As for Saturday night, Potter said she’s “definitely bringing in some surprise guests and friends,” adding: “I do think Saturday’s going to be quite a boisterous collective. We’ll probably try to hit songs we didn’t hit with the orchestra, but the orchestra set is surprisingly rocking.”
“I think Saturday does give us an opportunity to bring up guests and play other people’s music,” said Potter. “It’s not just about me. I’ve had 20-some-odd years of touring and throwing my voice out into the world.”
“I think it’s an opportunity for me to feature other artists, some really amazing folks.”
‘A sustainable pillar’
As with Grand Point North festivals in the past, Potter said this year’s event will feature more than just music.
“We’re gonna have some amazing performers, we’re gonna have some flash mob action, we’re gonna have some art installations,” she said, adding “the foodie world” and microbreweries to the list.
Proceeds from the festival will go to Grand Point Foundation “to regenerate and turn into programming,” she said. Recent events have included a free workshop for “Vermont’s rising creatives” with Potter and Senator Rocket of Eat Vermont at Waitsfield’s Big Picture Theater.
Potter projects the foundation to be a “sustainable pillar to remind people that when the world feels like it’s falling apart, civilization needs art,” she said. “It is a thing that stands tall, even in the darkest times.”
“I really feel like it’s why I was put on the planet, to have an opportunity to bring it to the forefront.”
While this summer was a relatively quiet one on the touring front for Potter — who also owns a home with Valentine in Topanga Canyon, California — highlights included performing with country superstars like longtime friend Kenny Chesney at The Sphere and opening for Chris Stapleton at Madison Square Garden.
Inspired after the Garden shows, Potter and her band took the train to her Vermont home to record some new music in their recently completed Sonic Forest Studios, a 10,000-square-foot recording studio that Valentine is now operating out of.
“The high of Madison Square Garden was so high, I wanted a memory of that window of time,” said Potter. “But it turned out that the band showed up with blazing colors and just nailed it, so we’ve got more than enough music for another record.”
Potter views the musical adventure as a “metaphor for what the foundation wants to do,” which includes connecting out-of-state artists to Vermont.
“Creative people come to Vermont to hide off in the woods and have their big ideas,” she said. “Why not share them in Vermont first, you know, take it straight out of the woods and onto the stage on the waterfront.”
“The objective of Grand Point Foundation will move out of state someday,” said Potter. “But I do not want to do that until I feel like I have put my boots on the ground and rolled up my sleeves.”
“It’s two hours in both directions to get across the state of Vermont,” she added. “That’s a lot of people hiding in the woods and making amazing art that deserves to be highlighted and uplifted and brought into this connectivity within our community.”
